opus-5.5.text:
I think the short answer is that the brain is remarkably bad at caring about the medium and remarkably good at caring about the signal. What I mean by that is, from a neuroscience perspective, your brain doesn't really have a special category for "this came through a screen" versus "this came through the air in a room." It's processing faces, voices, timing, reward, surprise. If those cues are there, a lot of the same machinery lights up.

There's a nice illustration of this from studies on synchrony. When two people are engaged in a good conversation, you can see their brain activity start to align, almost like they're dancing together. And what's interesting is that you get some of that alignment even when people are interacting over video, or when someone is just listening to a recorded story. It's weaker in some ways, but it's there. So the brain is willing to treat a mediated interaction as a real one, as long as it gets enough of the ingredients it's looking for.

The second part is habituation. Anything that's new feels strange, and then the brain very quickly updates its model of what's normal. Think about the telephone. When it first appeared, people were genuinely unsettled by hearing a disembodied voice of someone who wasn't there. Some people thought it was spooky. Within a generation, nobody thought twice about it. The same thing happened with texting, with video calls, and now it's happening with talking to AI. The brain is an efficiency machine. It doesn't want to spend energy being surprised by the same thing over and over, so it folds it into the baseline.

And the third piece, which I find the most fascinating and a little bit worrying, is that technology is often designed to hit our reward systems more precisely than real life does. A real friend doesn't always respond right away, isn't always in a good mood, doesn't always say the thing you want to hear. A device or a platform can be optimized to give you exactly the right dose of novelty and validation at exactly the right time. So it's not just that we accept it as normal. In some cases, the brain starts to prefer it, because it's cleaner, more predictable, more rewarding.

So the question I think we should be asking isn't really "will people accept this as normal," because the answer is almost always yes. The question is what we lose in the translation. Things like smell, touch, the tiny micro-expressions, the shared physical space. Those carry information we're not even consciously aware of, and we don't yet fully understand what happens to us over the long run when we swap them out.

r001.rationale: The response says people quickly update their sense of what is normal, stop thinking twice about once-strange technologies, and fold repeated experiences into the baseline.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the brain doesn't actually have a strong opinion about what's "real." It cares about prediction. If I'm talking to you and your face moves when I expect it to, your voice arrives roughly when my brain predicts it should, and you respond to the things I say in a way that fits the model I have of a person, then from the brain's point of view, that's a person. It doesn't check whether there's a cable in between.

We've seen this many times in history. When the telephone first appeared, people found it deeply strange. There were etiquette debates about whether it was rude to speak to someone you couldn't see. Within one generation, nobody thought about it. Same with text messaging, same with video calls. Each time, the first encounter feels thin, almost like a degraded version of the real thing, and then the brain simply recalibrates its baseline. What used to be the "poor copy" becomes the default, and we stop noticing the medium at all.

There's a mechanism behind this that I find really interesting. The brain is a very lazy organ, in a good way. It is constantly trying to spend less energy. Anything that repeats becomes automated and drops out of conscious awareness. When you first learned to drive, you were aware of every pedal. Now you arrive somewhere and barely remember the road. Mediated interaction goes through exactly that process. At first you notice the screen, the latency, the slightly odd eye contact. After a few hundred repetitions, those cues get filtered out as noise, and what remains is just the other person.

And then there's the social piece. Normal isn't something your brain decides alone. It's largely something you infer from the people around you. If everyone in your environment treats a Zoom call as a meeting, your brain adopts that as the standard almost immediately, because being out of sync with your group is far more costly, evolutionarily speaking, than being wrong about whether a conversation counts as real.

So I'd say the surprising thing isn't that we adapt. The surprising thing is how little actually needs to be present for the brain to accept something as a genuine interaction. A few of the right signals at the right time, and it fills in the rest. That's both reassuring and a little bit alarming, depending on who is controlling those signals.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated mediated interactions cause cues such as the screen and latency to be filtered out, so people stop noticing the medium.

astra-6.text:
I think because our sense of what’s normal is remarkably flexible. At first, you notice the technology. You’re talking to someone through a screen, and there’s a delay, and you’re looking at their face in this little box. But after a while, your attention shifts to the person and what they’re saying. The interface becomes background.

Think about a phone call. You hear a voice without a body, coming from someone who might be thousands of miles away. That’s a very unusual experience, but we don’t experience it as unusual anymore. We just think, ‘I’m talking to my mother.’

So I would distinguish normal from identical. A mediated interaction doesn’t have to feel exactly like being in the same room. It just has to become familiar and predictable enough that you stop thinking about how it works. And if the people around you use it too, it becomes part of how you expect life to happen.

r001.rationale: It says that with time attention shifts from the screen to the person, the interface becomes background, and people stop thinking about how the interaction works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of what we call normal is simply what our brain has learned to expect. The first time you speak to someone through a screen, it’s a strange thing: you can see them, you can hear them, but they’re not physically there. After enough repetitions, you stop thinking about the screen and start thinking about the person.

Our brains are very good at adapting to a consistent relationship between an action and an outcome. You say something, the other person responds, and the interaction starts to feel familiar. The technology becomes part of the background.

And then there’s a generational effect. If you grow up with that interaction, you don’t experience it as a replacement for something more natural. It’s simply one of the ways people communicate. That doesn’t mean every technology is equally good for us. It means that feeling normal and being good for us are two different questions.

r001.rationale: The response says that after repeated screen interactions, people stop thinking about the screen and focus on the person, so the technology fades into the background.
